RESEARCH — comprehensive learnings from the Institute's delivered policy documents (ACM Europe TPC products)

# 17-2 · What the policy documents actually say — learnings for /policy/

Date: 2026-08-01. Companion to `17-sheet-standards-policy.md` (the flagship page spec). Method: all ACM PDF binaries were downloaded with a browser UA and **read directly** (22 documents, primary-sourced); HTML-only ACM pages are Cloudflare-blocked and were **secondary-sourced via WebSearch** (marked ⓢ). Every claim below that matters for the page carries its source document. The two documents originally supplied as `acm-europe-tpc-cyber-reslience-comments-pdf` and `ustpc-approved-generative-ai-principles` are Cloudflare-blocked at those URLs but were recovered in full from alternate ACM PDF URLs (`europe-tpc-comments-cyber-resilience.pdf`, `principles-generative-ai.pdf` press release) — treat as primary.

## Headline findings (read this first)

1. **The "8 of 12" flagship claim is confirmed in the primary source, in ACM's own words.** The 2nd-draft GPAI response (15 Jan 2025) opens: *"Europe TPC is gratified that eight (8) out of twelve (12) initial recommendations made for the European Commission's First Draft are integrated in the main text of the Second Draft."* This is the strongest possible grounding — the adopting-organisation's own published statement, not self-attestation.
2. **Alejandro Saucedo is a named author/contributor on at least 11 of the delivered products**, and *principal author* of five of them: the AI Act comments (Aug 2021), the Data Act comments (May 2022), the UK AI framework comments (Sep 2022), the UK National Data Strategy comments (Dec 2020), and the Digital Principles comments (Sep 2021). He is one of three *lead authors* of the joint USTPC/Europe TPC Generative AI Principles (Jul 2023). Every one of these footnotes identifies him as "Chief Scientist at the Institute for Ethical AI & Machine Learning" — the Institute's name is in the public record of these instruments.
3. **The Institute's own MLSecOps framework is cited *into* the EU GPAI Code of Practice consultations.** Both GPAI responses (Rec 10) name "the Institute for Ethical ML's MLSecOps framework" with the link `https://ethical.institute/security.html` alongside MITRE ATT&CK, OWASP Top 10 ML and the UK NCSC ML principles as the reference cybersecurity taxonomies the Commission should build on. The practitioner-bridge argument of the /policy/ page is literally visible inside the policy record.

## Per-document record

### Track: EU — AI Act line

**Comments on the proposed AI Act (Harmonised Rules on AI)** — 5 Aug 2021 · responds to COM 2021/0106 (the original AI Act proposal). Principal authors: **Alejandro Saucedo** (Chief Scientist, Institute for Ethical AI & ML) and Chris Hankin (Imperial). Contributors incl. Dame Wendy Hall, Oliver Grau, Enrico Nardelli, Gerhard Schimpf. Positions: define the risk hierarchy precisely (Arts 6–7); define technical terms formally ("robustness", "accuracy" — adopt e.g. ISA/IEC 62443); import the Safety Assurance discipline for Art 15; regulate *self-modifying* systems post-approval and mandate detection of "operational divergence"; privacy floor = GDPR, constraints on continuous data collection in public, prohibitions on non-consensual facial recognition (Art 52); sandboxes must contain drift (Art 53); bridge the AI skills gap via Informatics for All (Art 59). Quotable: the operational-divergence passage — the earliest articulation in the record of continuous post-deployment oversight, five years before the agentic-oversight brief.

**EC AI White Paper consultation submission** — 19 Jun 2020 · responds to the Feb 2020 White Paper "AI — A European approach to excellence and trust" (the pre-legislative phase of the AI Act). Cover letter by Oliver Grau (then Chair). Questionnaire form; notable free-text answers: cybersecurity of production ML flagged as a top unlisted concern ("new loopholes may also be introduced… security flaws of machine learning systems being exploited"); ADM principles ("ADM is never neutral… ADM processes must be traceable so that they can be subjected to democratic control"); proportionate-to-risk compulsory requirements with an upfront evaluation step; names the Linux Foundation and NumFOCUS as partners the Commission should work with. This is the document that grounds "contributed through its *planning*" for the AI Act.

**1st GPAI Code of Practice comments** — 27 Nov 2024 · responds to the EC call for evidence (13 Nov 2024) on the "General Purpose AI Code of Practice for Providers of Models with Systemic Risk". **Twelve numbered recommendations.** Highlights: (1) keep the Code within its provider scope or formally extend it to deployers and re-balance the working groups; (2) systemic-risk mitigations should be a superset of high/de-minimis-risk practice, with MUST/SHOULD/COULD guidance and probability×impact calibration; (3–4) cover all modalities and ML-types, not just LLMs/image models; (5) standardised model-registration metadata and templates ("model-fair-use templates… similar to how standardised licenses exist for open source code"); (6) remove "automated use of models for AI R&D" as a systemic risk and qualify "long-horizon planning, forecasting" (demand forecasting is a common low-risk use); (7) evaluations must be measurable, reproducible, auditable with domain experts involved; (9) align with UK/US AI Safety Institutes; (10) build on MLSecOps / MITRE / OWASP / NCSC and task CEN-CENELEC/ETSI with EU AI-cybersecurity standards; (11) disambiguate "deployment" vs "release" per AI Act terminology; (12) proportion corrective measures to the capital impacted (human, natural, social, manufactured, financial). No named authors in the PDF.

**2nd GPAI Code of Practice comments** — 15 Jan 2025 · responds to the 2nd draft (19 Dec 2024). **Contains the verbatim 8-of-12 adoption statement** (see headline finding 1) plus a footnote naming the four not-yet-integrated recommendations (1, 2, 6, 11) that are re-urged for the third draft. Adds two net-new recommendations: (13) an **"incident register"** to record/track/resolve violations across copyright, security etc., retained ~5 years, managed at EC and/or organisational level; (14) extend security best practice (Measure 12.1) with an **incident-response plan for security breaches**. Rec 10 again cites the Institute's MLSecOps framework. Quotable stat for the impact band: "eight (8) out of twelve (12) initial recommendations… are integrated in the main text of the Second Draft."

**Guidelines on the definition of an AI system & prohibited practices** — Dec 2024 · responds to the EC call for evidence (13 Nov 2024) under Art 96(1) AI Act; 32-page full survey response. Core positions: the "statistical methods" carve-out from the AI-system definition should be reconsidered — **classification should follow the risk introduced by use of models, not the technical nature of the model** (the ensembles-of-logistic-regressions credit-scoring example shows the boundary is undefinable); the definition can catch non-AI software (automated refactoring, vulnerability scanners) and needs tangible in/out-of-scope examples; rated "varying levels of autonomy" and "infers… how to generate outputs" as the definition elements most needing clarification (10/10).

**Scientific panel of independent experts (EU) comments** — 15 Nov 2024 · responds to the draft Implementing Regulation establishing the AI Act's scientific panel. Three recommendations: scope the panel's work before fixing headcount; expertise must go beyond the purely technical (ethics, law, socio-economic, behavioural); the 3-experts-per-member-state cap should yield to where scarce high-demand expertise actually lives.

**Digital Omnibus on AI Regulation comments** — Jan 2026 · responds to the EC call for evidence on the Digital Omnibus AI proposal. Named authors: Gaston Besanson, Maciej Zuziak, **Alejandro Saucedo (The Institute for Ethical AI & Machine Learning)**, Francisco Mederios, Tom Romanoff. Article-by-article recommendations, unusually technical: **Art 4a** — the synthetic-data-first hierarchy for bias detection ignores statistical dependence (synthetic data inherits and can *mask* bias) and the differential-privacy/utility trade-off is mathematical, not an implementation gap — require documented calibration instead; **Art 6(4)** — "narrow" task exemptions are fragile for general-purpose models: require guardrails, runtime out-of-distribution monitoring and periodic re-validation ("narrowness is maintained rather than merely declared"); **Art 11(1)/63(1)** — SME simplification must mean streamlined format, never reduced technical records ("certain artifacts are irreducible for a meaningful audit"); **Art 50(7)/56(6)** — standardised, comparable watermarking/code-of-practice reporting with disclosed robustness metrics; **Arts 60/60a** — real-world testing needs hardware kill switches, drift-abort thresholds, incident reporting in hours not days; **Art 111(4)** — the Feb 2027 "marked and detectable" watermarking mandate is technically unmeetable; replace with a provenance standard plus disclosed false-positive/negative rates. Quotable: "This acknowledges that narrowness is maintained rather than merely declared."

**Response to the Art 50 transparency guidelines consultation** ⓢ — Jun 2026 (acm.org page `response-consultation-article-50-ai-act-06022026`). Authors verified previously: Besanson, Dixon, Milic-Frayling, **Saucedo**, Schimpf. Keep as listed in the sheet.

**Consultation on Regulation (EU) 2024/1689** ⓢ — Apr 2026 (page `consultation-on-regulation-on-eu-ai-act-eu-2024-1689-04082026`). Page exists; content not retrievable (Cloudflare). An HPCwire syndication headline describes it as "ACM Policy Group Proposes Fundamental Rethinking of AI Regulation in Europe" — use title+link only, no claims about content.

**Calibrating Oversight for Agentic Frontier Models** ⓢ — 27 Apr 2026 (page `calibrating-oversight-agentic-frontier-models-04272026`). Secondary summary: agentic AI's systemic risks are only partially addressed by the AI Act; the brief identifies the gaps and recommends making oversight **continuous and dynamic**. This pairs directly with KAOS and the 2021 "operational divergence" position — the through-line for the practitioner-bridge section.

**Reflections on draft prEN 18282 (Cybersecurity Specifications for AI Systems)** ⓢ — (page `reflections-draft-pren-18282`; the CEN draft standard supporting the AI Act). Secondary summary: welcomes the draft; recognises AI security exceeds conventional ICT security (attack surfaces via training/validation/inference data, model artefacts, prompts, agents, third-party models); recommends strengthening AI supply-chain security, treating **data governance as a cybersecurity requirement**, adding controls for **retrieval-augmented, tool-connected and agentic systems**, recognising AI-assisted security testing (reproducibility, validation, containment), and defining indicators for incidents and near-misses. Extremely on-brand for /frameworks/security/.

### Track: EU — digital acts

**Data Act comments** — 13 May 2022 · responds to the proposed Data Act (COM(2022) 68). **Principal author: Alejandro Saucedo**; contributors Hankin, Knowles, Milic-Frayling, Nardelli, Solmaz. Three key recommendations: bring **metadata** into scope where needed to actually consume the data (Arts 2–3); the Act must "define, address, and preclude or minimise foreseeable environmental impacts" — actively **discourage proof-of-work distributed ledgers** whose energy consumption "necessarily will undermine the high level aims of the European Green Deal" (Arts 11, 30); avoid needless complexity/cost in data-provision duties, and fix cloud-switching via **industry-wide standards for data ingestion formats, protocols and data-models** because the real switching barrier is technical, not contractual (Arts 23–26).

**DSA initial comments** — undated (2020, pre-adoption; Hankin as Chair contact) · 1-page position ahead of the DSA's adoption. Two points: automated content moderation has inherent limitations and biases that legislation must safeguard against; the "vetted researcher" regime (Art 31) must not exclude qualified researchers through overly restrictive data-storage provisions.

**DSA data-access (Art 40) call-for-evidence comments** — 23 May 2023 · researchers' access to VLOP/VLOSE data. Positions: transparency needs more than data — **"the roots of harmful undesired outcomes may be traced not only to data, but to machine learning models and system level components"**, so researchers need visibility into processing architecture and intra-system APIs (cites Twitter's open-sourced recommender and the hard-coded political-leaning logic found only because the *code* was public — a ready-made open-source-transparency exhibit); vetting should prioritise security/privacy; follow Open Data best practice; fund an open consortium for systemic-risk research methods.

**DSA Delegated Regulation on data access — draft act comments** — 2024 · responds to the draft Delegated Regulation under Art 40 DSA. Named authors: Deshpande, Di Biasi, Zuziak, Rožanec, Nagy, **Saucedo** (+ Medeiros, Mizera-Pietraszko). Positions: broadly supportive; use ORCID/ROR for researcher vetting; objective, member-state-consistent criteria instead of DSC discretion; open-data-spirit access with security/anonymity carve-outs; infrastructure held to SOC 2 / ISO 27001 / NIST CSF; data providers must disclose synthetic-data use, data age, and "cleanliness"/pre-processing estimates (60–80% of researcher time is pre-processing); proposed **Data Readiness Levels** on the DSA portal; fix the Art 8(6) "prove you can't get the data elsewhere" ground for dismissal; mediation-cost good-faith fix (Art 13).

**Cyber Resilience Act comments** — Jan 2023 (dated by the G7 survey's footnote as 23 Jan 2023) · responds to COM(2022) 454. Principal author: Chris Hankin. Positions: the **open-source exclusion may backfire** — vendors could shelter behind OSS components; extend scope to commercial software on open-source SDKs/APIs (Log4J, SolarWinds); the Class I/II critical-product lists need a higher level of abstraction and a faster revision mechanism; harmonise product-lifetime duties with right-to-repair; clarify white-labelled hardware; **SBOMs are central** — set minimum content standards in the Act; reference ENISA's Cybersecurity Skills Framework for the assessor shortage; index penalties over time; add vulnerability-reporting standards and timelines.

**European Digital Principles supplemental comments** — 1 Sep 2021 · responds to the EC consultation on a set of European Digital Principles. **Principal author: Alejandro Saucedo.** Positions: codify what "access" minimally means, secure-by-design for critical services; make universal Informatics education a formal Digital Principle; human-in-the-loop touchpoints and design-stage bias removal wherever AI mediates the online environment; digital identity with data-minimising authentication; climate "respect" = measured carbon footprints across design→manufacture→supply chain and net-zero ICT by mid-century; "algorithmic systems" is the wrong term — use "digital systems".

**ETPC survey responses (G7 Hiroshima Guiding Principles)** — 20 Oct 2023 · responds to the EC stakeholder survey on the 11 draft G7 Guiding Principles for organisations developing advanced AI systems. Rates all 11 principles 5/5; extends scope to internal operators/users; endorses monitoring via internationally trusted organisations + national bodies + self-assessment (rejects "no monitoring"); asks the G7 text to absorb the ACM Responsible Algorithmic Systems principles (legitimacy/competency, minimising harm, interpretability, contestability/auditability, accountability) and the Generative AI principles on Ownership and Correctability.

### Track: United Kingdom

**UK AI regulatory framework comments ("Establishing a pro-innovation approach to regulating AI")** — 23 Sep 2022 · responds to Command Paper CP 728. **Principal author: Alejandro Saucedo** (footnote 1: "Engineering Director at Seldon Technologies and Chief Scientist at the Institute for Ethical AI & Machine Learning"); contributors Hankin, Knowles, Milic-Frayling. **Four general recommendations**: (I) environmental risks and impacts must explicitly be addressed; (II) AI regulation must be internationally compatible/interoperable (Safe-Harbor-style mechanism suggested); (III) define the imprecise cross-sectoral terms — "fairness", "explainable", "transparent", "risk"; (IV) the framework's development must remain a highly transparent process — and the UK should establish its own **High-Level Expert Group for AI**, emulating the EC's. Quotable: UK policy could become "a blueprint for how the responsible development and deployment of AI technologies at a national level can lead to a thriving economy and healthy AI ecosystem."

**UK AI paper comments ("AI regulation: a pro-innovation approach" White Paper)** — 20 Jun 2023 · follow-up consultation response. **States in ACM's own words: "Europe TPC is gratified that the latter three of these four suggestions were accepted and are reflected in the present White Paper"** — i.e. 3 of the 4 initial recommendations adopted, with the environmental one re-urged and extended (beyond carbon to land degradation from mining and water for cooling; cites the 700,000-litre GPT-3 training-water figure). Adds **ten new numbered recommendations (5–14)**: generative-AI-specific requirements per the Generative AI Principles + legitimacy/contestability; align "security" with NCSC ML security principles; adopt the OECD/EC definition of AI; informatics education for the AI workforce; **policy and regulatory guidelines for open model artifacts, open-source frameworks and data**; harmonise the UK risk framework with the EU's four-level risk pyramid; whistleblowing/redress channels proportionate to risk; DSA-style platform-data access for transparency research; monitor consumer trust (Stanford AI Index-style); sector sandboxes for long-procurement-cycle industries. Total across the two UK AI documents: **14 numbered recommendations** — the documentary basis of the "13 of 14" claim (see evidence status).

**UK National Data Strategy comments** — 2 Dec 2020 · responds to the 9 Sep 2020 NDS consultation. **Principal author: Alejandro Saucedo** (Chief Scientist, "UK-based Institute for Ethical AI & Machine Learning"); contributors Hankin, Knowles, Williamson. Positions: COVID data collected with purpose-specific consent; open datasets drive urban/social research; consult those with protected characteristics directly ("the true experts are those individuals who may be marginalised"); explicit mandates so rural/scarce-data regions are represented in datasets feeding policy decisions.

### Track: United Nations / global

**UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI consultation** — 14 Feb 2025 · responds to the UN Office for Digital and Emerging Technologies call for evidence on the Panel + Global Dialogue on AI Governance. Positions: mandate = evidence-based human-centric risk/benefit assessment, governance frameworks, security assessments, sustainable development; **≤30 top experts**, diverse geographically and across the 8 ACM-CCS AI fields plus humanities; nomination committee, sunset clauses, conflict-of-interest disclosure; **IPCC-inspired UN-led AI Risk & Impact Reports** at least twice-yearly plus short-notice ex-ante convening for high-impact events; sustainability/energy-usage reporting as a standing assessment; the UN should form formal partnerships with ACM, IEEE and the AI safety institutes; "produce inclusive AI governance, not just industry led".

**EU–US TTC Terminology and Taxonomy for AI comments** — 21 Nov 2023 · responds to the TTC WG1 first-edition taxonomy. Term-by-term corrections: delete "imitating the way that humans learn" from Machine Learning ("there is no scientific consensus as to how humans learn"); define true/false positives, recall, precision, F-measures under Accuracy; broaden Algorithm beyond step-by-step to concurrent deep-learning processes; make "Human Values for AI" concrete (whose values, embedded how); replace "human-centric" with **"human-centered AI"** — "systems [that] work in partnership with human beings and enhance human capabilities rather than replace human intelligence"; socio-technical systems defined as a two-way society↔technology relationship; add dataset provenance to Opacity.

**Statement on Principles for Responsible Algorithmic Systems** (`final-joint-ai-statement-update.pdf`) — 26 Oct 2022 · joint ACM Europe TPC + US TPC statement (updates the 2017 joint statement). Lead authors Baeza-Yates & Matthews; **important contributions: … Alejandro Saucedo** (named). Defines **nine instrumental principles**: 1 Legitimacy and competency · 2 Minimizing harm · 3 Security and privacy · 4 Transparency · 5 Interpretability and explainability · 6 Maintainability · 7 Contestability and auditability · 8 Accountability and responsibility · 9 **Limiting environmental impacts**. Notable lines: "Projects with no clear scientific basis (e.g., inferring personality traits from facial images) should not be deployed"; "Public scrutiny of the data and models provides maximum opportunity for correction"; "Operators of AI systems should be held responsible for the decisions they make… regardless of whether algorithmic tools are used"; impact-tiered transparency; "It is difficult to expect market forces to incentivize private companies to balance trade-offs that involve risks to individuals and to society."

**Principles for the Development, Deployment, and Use of Generative AI Technologies** — approved Jun 2023, released 11 Jul 2023 · joint USTPC + Europe TPC (ACM Technology Policy Council). **Lead authors: Ravi Jain, Jeanna Matthews, and Alejandro Saucedo.** Eight principles — four GenAI-specific: Limits and guidance on deployment and use (no high-risk system without a human in the loop and consensus that benefits outweigh harms; risk-level hierarchy), Ownership (IP law doesn't yet account for GenAI), Personal data control (opt-out of training data), Correctability (public error repositories); four adapted: Transparency, Auditability and contestability, Limiting environmental impact, Heightened security and privacy. Core line: "Existing mechanisms and modes for avoiding such harm likely will not suffice."

### Track: Sustainability

**Policy Brief on the EU AI Act for True Environmental Accountability** (`acm_climate_disclosure_final.pdf`) — 2 Jun 2025 · policy brief on the enacted AI Act's climate provisions. Lead authors Hacker, Alder, Ebert, Herbrich; **contributors: Knowles, Kaack, Alejandro Saucedo**. Five primary recommendations: (1) **inference-phase energy transparency** — the Act "turns a blind eye to the largest source of direct energy consumption — the everyday use of the model by millions of customers"; extend Annexes IV/XI/XII, disclose GPU-hours/PDU/PUE; (2) include indirect GHG emissions (e.g. ML for fossil-fuel exploration); (3) include water-consumption estimates; (4) **remove the open-source exemption for climate disclosures** above thresholds (e.g. 10^23 FLOPs or >1M users) — "the public availability of model weights should not exempt developers from disclosing environmental metrics" (note: a pro-disclosure position the Institute co-signed *about* open-source models — phrase carefully on the OSS-friendly site); (5) standard measurement methodology (cumulative server level with PDUs × PUE; task-specific inference benchmarks). Plus: a **public climate-metrics registry under open-data principles**; secondary: sustainability risk assessments in Arts 9/55, time-of-use compute constraints, renewable-buildout obligations, tradable "AI energy budgets". Quotable: "As in other areas, sunlight is often the best disinfectant."

**Powering Europe's Digital Transformation: A Roadmap to Greener Data Centers** (`acm_data_center_final.pdf`) — 2 Jun 2025 · policy brief on the EED (EU 2023/1791) + Delegated Regulation (EU 2024/1364). Same author group; **contributor: Alejandro Saucedo**. Five recommendations: binding PUE targets (Singapore ≤1.3, Australia 1.4, California/China 1.5 as comparators) + renewable quotas + **per-customer energy/water disclosure** so AI developers can choose hosts on sustainability; lower the reporting threshold 500 kW → 300 kW with tiered duties; WUE benchmarks (<2.0 m³/MWh Singapore comparator) and AI Act/EED alignment on water + indirect GHG; an anonymised EU registry with granular data, measurements over estimates; plan for AI load-spikes via load shifting/dynamic allocation. Frames the AI Continent Action Plan's "gigafactories" as needing Green Deal-consistent guardrails. **Spanish twin exists** (`acm-data-center-final-spanish`, HTML) — note for the record only.

## Cross-document synthesis — the Institute's recurring policy positions

These eight theses recur across the record and are the substance the /policy/ page should radiate. Each lists its supporting documents.

**T1 · Oversight must be continuous, not a one-time approval.** From "operational divergence" detection for self-modifying systems (AI Act 2021) → post-release monitoring and correction requests (GPAI-1 Rec 5) → the incident register + incident-response plan (GPAI-2 Recs 13–14) → runtime out-of-distribution monitoring and periodic re-validation of "narrow" exemptions, kill switches and drift-abort thresholds for real-world testing (Omnibus 2026) → "continuous and dynamic" oversight of agentic frontier models (Apr 2026 ⓢ). This is the single strongest through-line, and it maps 1:1 onto KAOS's runtime-governance thesis.

**T2 · Regulate the risk of the use, not the technique.** The AI-definition response's core argument (risk-based classification "as opposed to the technical nature of the models"; the statistical-methods carve-out is unprincipled); the 2020 White Paper answer (scrutiny "proportionate to the risk involved" with a mandatory upfront evaluation); GPAI-2 Rec 2 (risk tiers = frequency × severity, systemic-risk duties a superset of lower tiers); Responsible Algorithmic Systems (risks "proportional to the specific problems being addressed", impact-tiered transparency); UK 2022 Rec III (define "risk" itself).

**T3 · Define your terms — precision is a policy instrument.** Undefined technical terms is the most repeated critique in the record: AI Act 2021 (robustness, accuracy, "free of errors"); UK 2022 (fairness, explainable, transparent, risk); TTC taxonomy 2023 (the entire document); GPAI Recs 11 (deployment vs release) and 3–4 (modality scope); Omnibus (what "simplified" and "narrow" mean). The offer to policymakers writes itself: the Institute reviews draft instruments at the level where a single undefined word becomes an enforcement problem.

**T4 · Evaluations and audits must be measurable, reproducible and auditable — and some records are irreducible.** GPAI Recs 7–8 (measurable/reproducible/auditable evaluations, effectiveness parameters instead of a "gold standard"); Omnibus Arts 11(1)/63(1) ("certain artifacts are irreducible for a meaningful audit"); Responsible Algorithmic Systems P7 (record data/models/decisions so results can be replicated); GenAI Principles (auditability and contestability, public error repositories); DSA data-access work (immutable logs, Data Readiness Levels).

**T5 · Security of ML systems is its own discipline — and the Institute's frameworks are part of the reference set.** GPAI Recs 10+14 (MLSecOps/MITRE/OWASP/NCSC as the taxonomy base; CEN-CENELEC/ETSI EU standards; breach-response plans); prEN 18282 reflections ⓢ (AI attack surfaces beyond ICT security, data governance as a security requirement, agentic/RAG controls); CRA comments (OSS-exclusion backfire risk, SBOM minimum standards); UK 2023 Rec 6 (align "security" with NCSC ML principles); White Paper 2020 (ML security flagged unprompted as a missing concern); Responsible Algorithmic Systems P3 and GenAI "heightened security and privacy".

**T6 · Open source is load-bearing infrastructure that policy must engage, not exempt-and-ignore.** UK 2023 Rec 9 (regulatory guidelines *for* open model artifacts, open-source frameworks and data — PyTorch/TF/sklearn named); GPAI Rec 5 footnote (model-fair-use templates "similar to how standardised licenses exist for open source code (e.g. Apache, MIT)") — an EAL-adjacent idea in an EU consultation; CRA (excluding OSS creates a loophole; protect the ecosystem by scoping dependencies properly); DSA 2023 (Twitter's open-sourced recommender as proof that code-level scrutiny finds what I/O audits cannot); White Paper 2020 (Linux Foundation, NumFOCUS as named partners); climate brief (open-source models shouldn't be exempt from *climate* disclosure — disclosure-parity, framed with protections for collaborative innovation).

**T7 · Compute has a body: energy, water, land — and inference is the blind spot.** The deepest sustained line after oversight: Data Act 2022 (discourage proof-of-work ledgers; count energy as a compliance cost); UK 2022 Rec I → UK 2023 (the one unadopted recommendation, re-urged and extended to water and mining); Digital Principles 1.8 (measured footprints, net-zero ICT); Responsible Algorithmic Systems P9 and GenAI principle 7 (environmental impact as a *principle*); climate brief (inference > training energy; open-data registry); data-center brief (binding PUE/WUE, per-customer disclosure); UN panel (sustainability as a standing global assessment). Notably, the Institute kept pressing the one recommendation governments kept declining — good-faith evidence the page can use ("we publish what was adopted *and* what wasn't").

**T8 · Transparency is for the public, and must be paired with redress.** Public registries recur everywhere: model incident register (GPAI-2), climate-metrics registry, data-center registry, GenAI error repositories, DSA public dashboards + API. And transparency is never an endpoint: "Transparency must be paired with processes for accountability that enable stakeholders… to seek meaningful redress" (Responsible Algorithmic Systems); contestability/whistleblowing channels (UK 2023 Q4); mediation fairness (DSA delegated); "ADM processes must be traceable so that they can be subjected to democratic control" (White Paper 2020).

Two auxiliary threads worth one line each on the page: **international interoperability** (UK Rec II, TTC taxonomy, GPAI Rec 9 AISI alignment, UN panel — regulatory alignment as an innovation enabler) and **human-in-the-loop as the qualifier of dangerous capability** (GPAI footnote, GenAI principle 1, Digital Principles 1.5, White Paper facial-recognition answer).

## Evidence status for the flagship claims

**"8 of 12 recommendations adopted — EU 2nd-draft GPAI Code of Practice": CONFIRMED, primary source.** `acm-europetpc-consultation-2024---2nd-general-purpose-ai-code-of-practice-1.pdf`, p.1, verbatim. The page can cite the ACM document itself instead of (or alongside) the LinkedIn post — a materially stronger evidence link. Precision note for copy: the eight were integrated into the *second draft main text*; four (Recs 1, 2, 6, 11) were re-urged for the third draft.

**"13 of 14 recommendations adopted — UK AI Regulatory Proposal": PARTIALLY GROUNDED; final ratio rests on owner attestation.** What the documents themselves establish: the two UK AI submissions together contain exactly **14 numbered recommendations** (4 initial in Sep 2022 + 10 new in Jun 2023), and ACM's own Jun 2023 document confirms **3 of the 4 initial recommendations were "accepted and are reflected in the present White Paper"**, with the environmental recommendation the standing exception. The step from 3/4-plus-10-pending to 13/14 (i.e., 10 of the 10 new ones subsequently adopted, environment still out) is not documented in anything read here — it presumably tracks the UK's Feb 2024 consultation response, which post-dates these PDFs. Recommendation: keep 13/14 with the ⚠ conservative marker until the owner supplies the post-2023 mapping, or phrase as "3 of 4 initial recommendations adopted into the UK White Paper, with 14 delivered in total" if a fully self-evidencing line is preferred. Do not silently swap evidence links between the two UK claims.

**"Contributed to every major European digital policy through its planning, creation and execution": SUBSTANTIALLY GROUNDED with a phrasing caution.** Delivered, dated submissions exist for: the AI Act at its planning stage (White Paper 2020), proposal stage (Aug 2021), and execution stage (definition guidelines 2024, GPAI CoP 2024–25, scientific panel 2024, Art 50 2026, 2024/1689 consultation 2026, Omnibus 2026) — the three-phase framing genuinely holds *for the AI Act*. Data Act (2022, proposal stage), DSA (2020 pre-adoption + 2023/2024 implementation), CRA (2023, proposal stage), UK proposal (2020 NDS + 2022 + 2023) each have at least one phase. "Every major European digital policy" is defensible for the named five instruments; keep the sentence enumerating them (as the spec already does) rather than open-ended.

**Attribution chain (Institute vs ACM): strong.** These are ACM Europe TPC products, but the Institute's claim to them is documented three ways: (a) Saucedo named as principal/lead author or contributor on 11+ of them, always with the Institute affiliation in the document; (b) the Institute's own framework cited inside the GPAI responses; (c) the founding-chair role (volunteer record, per sheet 17). The page's existing "All via the ACM Europe Technology Policy Committee" framing is the honest and sufficient formula — never phrase as "the Institute submitted".

## Feed-forward — what should surface where
